title: Why NoSQL
summary: Why teams reach for NoSQL, the four data-model families, and the two biggest misconceptions that get NoSQL chosen for the wrong reasons.

slides.markdown:
"NoSQL" isn't one technology — it's an umbrella for several data-model families (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) that all made a deliberate trade: give up some of the relational model's guarantees or query flexibility in exchange for horizontal scale, flexible schema, or a data shape that maps directly to how the application uses it.

The interview-relevant skill isn't naming NoSQL databases — it's matching a workload's actual access pattern to the family built for it, and knowing precisely what you give up to get there.

slides.sectionTitle: The real drivers: scale, flexible schema, developer velocity
slides.markdown:
Three forces actually push teams toward NoSQL, and naming the right one for a given scenario is the interview signal. **Scale** — a relational database's write throughput on a single primary eventually caps out (tens of thousands of writes/sec is a common ceiling), while many NoSQL stores are built to partition writes across nodes from day one. **Flexible schema** — when a document's shape varies a lot or evolves fast (different attributes per product category, say), forcing every field into fixed columns means constant migrations. **Developer velocity** — mapping an application object directly to a stored document, with no ORM translation layer, is genuinely faster to build against for many teams.

A staff-level answer names which of these three is actually driving the decision for a given system — "we need NoSQL" without naming one is a red flag.

| Family | Access pattern | Example | Sweet spot |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key-value | Get/put by a single key, no query language | Redis, DynamoDB | Caching, session storage, feature flags |
| Document | Nested JSON/BSON, secondary indexes on fields | MongoDB, Couchbase | Content that varies in shape, user profiles, catalogs |
| Wide-column | Rows keyed by partition + clustering key, sparse columns | Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable | Massive write throughput, time-series, event logs |
| Graph | Nodes and edges, traversal queries | Neo4j, Amazon Neptune | Deep relationship queries — social graphs, fraud rings |

**How to decide:** ask "what's the primary query, and how deep does it traverse relationships?" — a single-key fetch points at key-value, a multi-hop relationship query points at graph, and everything in between usually lands on document or wide-column depending on write volume.

Relational modeling normalizes data into small tables joined at query time. NoSQL modeling typically does the opposite: it groups everything an application usually reads together into one **aggregate** — one document, one wide-column row — so a single read (often a single key lookup) returns everything needed, no joins required.

An `order` aggregate in a document store might embed the shipping address, line items, and payment summary directly inside the order document, even though a relational schema would split those into four normalized tables. The trade: reads are fast and simple (one fetch), but updating the customer's address on every past order embedding it means updating many documents instead of one row.

This is the mental shift most engineers coming from relational backgrounds get wrong first: **model around the read**, not around eliminating duplication.

**Wrong belief:** "NoSQL databases have no schema, so we don't need to plan our data model."

**Why it's wrong:** the schema still exists — it's just enforced by the **application** at read time instead of by the database at write time. This is called **schema-on-read** versus SQL's **schema-on-write**. If a `user` document's shape changes (a field renamed, a nested object restructured), every piece of code reading old-format documents has to handle both shapes, because the database won't reject or migrate them for you.

**Correct model:** "schemaless" NoSQL stores trade *when* the schema is enforced, not *whether* one exists. Skipping data-model planning because "it's schemaless" just moves inconsistent, half-migrated documents into production, discovered only when application code crashes on an unexpected shape.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: choosing NoSQL to avoid learning SQL
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Joins and normalization are complicated, so a document database will make our data layer simpler."

**Why it's wrong:** if your data is genuinely relational — orders reference customers, customers have addresses, addresses are shared — that relational structure doesn't disappear when you pick a document store; it just moves from the database's join engine into your application code, which now has to fetch related documents in multiple round trips and keep denormalized copies consistent by hand. Teams that make this switch to "avoid complexity" often end up rebuilding a worse, ad-hoc version of what a relational database did for free.

**Correct model:** choose NoSQL because the access pattern and scale genuinely fit one of its families (§4), not because SQL joins feel hard — a relational database with well-designed indexes handles the vast majority of application workloads correctly and simply.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: data-model shapes side by side
slides.markdown:
![Four panels showing the same customer and order data as a key-value blob, a nested document, a wide-column row, and a graph of connected nodes](assets/data-model-shapes.svg)

The same logical data — a customer who placed an order — looks structurally different in each family: an opaque blob, a nested tree, a sparse wide row, or two connected nodes. None of these shapes is "more correct"; each optimizes for a different access pattern.

Seeing this side by side is usually the fastest way to internalize why "NoSQL" isn't a single alternative to relational modeling — it's four different alternatives.

slides.sectionTitle: The consistency trade most NoSQL stores make explicit
slides.markdown:
Many NoSQL stores (Cassandra, DynamoDB) make the CAP-theorem trade-off a first-class, tunable setting rather than hiding it. Cassandra lets you choose **consistency level per query** — `ONE` (fast, might read stale data from a lagging replica), `QUORUM` (majority of replicas agree, stronger but slower), `ALL` (every replica, strongest and slowest). DynamoDB similarly offers eventually-consistent reads (cheaper, default) versus strongly-consistent reads (costs more, consumes more read capacity).

This matters because it turns a systems-design abstraction into a concrete per-query decision: a "like count" display can tolerate `ONE`/eventually-consistent reads with no user-visible harm, while a "check current inventory before charging a card" read generally shouldn't.

Interview signal: naming the actual mechanism (a tunable consistency level per operation) rather than a vague "NoSQL sacrifices consistency for availability" shows you understand it's a dial, not a fixed trade.

The honest counterpart to "why NoSQL" is knowing when it's the wrong call. Workloads with genuinely complex, ad-hoc, multi-table queries (financial reporting, arbitrary analyst SQL) lean relational, because NoSQL's fast path is usually a small set of known access patterns baked into the schema — queries outside that set are slow or impossible without a full redesign.

Strict multi-row transactional integrity (a bank transfer debiting one account and crediting another atomically) is native to relational engines via ACID transactions; most NoSQL stores either lack multi-document transactions entirely or added them later with real performance cost (MongoDB's multi-document transactions, for instance, are notably more expensive than single-document writes).

The honest framing for an interview: NoSQL trades query flexibility for scale and shape-fit along known access patterns — if you don't know your access patterns yet, or need arbitrary querying, that trade is usually a bad one.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: when "one primary can't keep up" actually becomes true
slides.markdown:
Worth grounding in real numbers rather than vibes: a well-tuned single Postgres primary can often sustain **5,000-20,000 writes/sec** depending on row size, indexing, and hardware — plenty for the overwhelming majority of applications, including many that assume they need NoSQL from day one.

Systems that genuinely exceed this — ad-tech bid logging, IoT telemetry at millions of devices, global-scale social feeds — are the ones for which wide-column stores' partition-per-node write scaling (each node handling its own slice, no single write bottleneck) earns its complexity.

The interview-useful habit: before reaching for NoSQL on scale grounds, estimate the actual required write rate and compare it to what a well-tuned relational primary (plus read replicas, plus caching) can plausibly sustain — "we'll eventually need to scale" isn't the same as "we need it now," and premature NoSQL adoption trades away transactional simplicity for a scale problem you may never hit.

slides.sectionTitle: Polyglot persistence: using more than one at once
slides.markdown:
Real systems at scale rarely pick exactly one database for everything — this is called **polyglot persistence**. A typical e-commerce backend might use Postgres for orders and payments (needs ACID transactions), Redis for session state and rate limiting (needs sub-millisecond key-value access), Elasticsearch for product search (needs full-text and faceted queries neither of the others do well), and Cassandra for clickstream/event logging (needs to absorb huge write volume).

The trade-off is operational: each additional data store is another system to run, monitor, back up, and keep a team skilled in — and keeping data consistent across them (e.g., search index lagging behind the source of truth) becomes its own engineering problem, usually solved with change-data-capture pipelines.

The staff-level framing: polyglot persistence is a deliberate trade of operational complexity for per-workload fit — not a default to reach for on a small system where one well-chosen database would do.
